title: Drowning (adults and children)
subject: emergency
summary: Drowning kills by hypoxia, so ventilation comes first: open the airway, give 5 initial rescue breaths (with oxygen if available), then standard CPR. After rescue, treat hypoxaemia with oxygen, CPAP/NIV or intubation with PEEP, manage hypothermia, and observe for delayed respiratory deterioration. Antibiotics and steroids are not routine.

sections.title: Recognise
items: Drowning is respiratory impairment from submersion or immersion in liquid; outcomes are fatal or non-fatal (with or without morbidity). Avoid the terms near-drowning, dry drowning and secondary drowning.
Hypoxia from aspiration and laryngospasm is the core injury, causing surfactant loss and pulmonary oedema, then bradycardia and asphyxial cardiac arrest.

Look for a precipitant: seizure, arrhythmia (long QT), hypoglycaemia, alcohol or drugs, trauma (diving into shallow water), hypothermia, and inadequate supervision or non-accidental injury in young children.
India: young children drown in ponds, wells, water tanks and buckets near home; floods, monsoon and boating incidents cause many adult deaths.

sections.title: Rescue and resuscitation
items: Rescuer safety first: reach or throw rather than go in; in-water rescue and in-water rescue breathing only by trained rescuers.

Remove from the water promptly (horizontal if possible). Immobilise the spine only with a trauma mechanism (diving, water sports, fall) or focal neurology, and never at the cost of delaying airway care.
Not breathing normally: open the airway and give 5 initial rescue breaths with 100% oxygen if available, then CPR 30:2 (children: 15:2 by trained rescuers). Compression-only CPR is not appropriate.
Do not try to drain water (no abdominal thrusts or head-down tipping). Regurgitation is common: turn to the side, suction and continue.
Use the lowest effective bag-mask pressures to limit gastric inflation; early tracheal intubation by a skilled operator; dry the chest before defibrillation.
Standard ALS drugs and doses. Consider ECPR for refractory arrest where available. If hypothermic, follow the hypothermia protocol and do not stop resuscitation until rewarmed.

sections.title: Hospital management
items: Oxygen to keep SpO2 94 to 98%. Rising work of breathing or hypoxaemia: CPAP/NIV or high-flow nasal oxygen if alert and protecting the airway; intubate if GCS falls, the patient tires, or non-invasive support fails.
Ventilate with lung-protective settings (tidal volume 6 mL/kg predicted body weight, plateau pressure below 30 cmH2O) and PEEP titrated to oxygenation; drowning lung injury behaves like ARDS.
Shock: correct hypoxia first; crystalloid boluses (children 10 mL/kg) and inotropes guided by echocardiography. Fresh versus salt water does not change management.
No routine antibiotics (only for grossly contaminated water such as sewage or floodwater, or signs of infection); no steroids; no surfactant.
Treat seizures and hypoglycaemia; pass a nasogastric tube to decompress the stomach in ventilated patients; rewarm if hypothermic.

sections.title: Investigations
items: Blood gas, glucose, electrolytes, renal function, CBC, lactate, core temperature.
ECG for QT prolongation or arrhythmia as a cause; chest X-ray if any respiratory signs (changes can lag by hours).
CT head and cervical spine only with trauma or altered consciousness; alcohol and toxicology screen as indicated.

sections.title: Disposition
items: Asymptomatic or mild (normal mentation, normal respiratory rate and SpO2 on air, clear chest): observe in the ED; paediatric evidence supports discharge after about 8 hours of observation if still well.

Admit any patient with hypoxaemia, crackles, abnormal chest X-ray, altered consciousness, oxygen need, or a history of arrest or prolonged submersion; ICU if NIV, intubation or post-arrest care is needed.

Post-arrest survivors: post-cardiac arrest care with temperature control and multimodal neuroprognostication at 72 hours or more; submersion duration is the strongest predictor, but do not prognosticate at the scene.

sections.title: Prevention
items: Cover or fence wells, ponds and water tanks; supervised day care (for example anganwadi creches) for pre-school children; never leave young children alone near buckets or tubs.
Teach school-age children basic swimming and water safety; life jackets on boats and ferries; flood preparedness; no alcohol around water.
Train families and community first responders in CPR that includes rescue breaths.

sections.title: Pitfalls
items: Compression-only CPR or delayed ventilation.
Routine collar and spinal board delaying airway management when there is no trauma mechanism.
Early discharge of a patient with cough, tachypnoea or low SpO2; deterioration can occur over hours.
Stopping resuscitation early in a cold drowned child.

drugs.name: Oxygen
drugs.dose: 100% via bag-mask or reservoir mask initially; titrate to SpO2 94 to 98%
drugs.notes: CPAP/NIV or HFNO if hypoxaemia persists.

drugs.name: Adrenaline (epinephrine) in cardiac arrest
drugs.dose: Adult 1 mg IV or IO; child 10 micrograms/kg IV or IO (maximum 1 mg); every 3 to 5 minutes
drugs.notes: Standard ALS/PALS. Withhold below 30 degrees C core temperature (hypothermia protocol).

drugs.name: Crystalloid (0.9% saline or balanced)
drugs.dose: Child 10 mL/kg IV bolus, reassess; adult 250 to 500 mL boluses with reassessment
drugs.notes: Warm the fluid if hypothermic. Avoid overload in injured lungs.
